newsitem.title: USA: Mfg improves, but Nov output data said overstated.
newsitem.headline: Mfg improves, but Nov output data said overstated.

text.p: Manufacturing activity continued to improve in November, but the latest output data overstate current strength, having gotten a one-time boost from the end of the General Motors strike, analysts said.
Industrial production jumped 0.9 percent in November, above the 0.6 percent rise seen in a Reuters poll. The capacity utilization rate rose to 83.3 percent from a revised 82.9 percent in October.
"Manufacturing is only doing slightly better," said PaineWebber Inc. chief economist Maury Harris.

The Federal Reserve reported that half of the November increase was due to a rebound in GM motor vehicle production. Another 0.2 percent of the growth was due to utilities output, which was boosted by unusually cold weather.

"We had one strong month. It is nothing to get excited about," said John Ryding, senior economist at Bear Stearns & Co, noting that clearer picture of production can be derived by averaging October and November figures.
October output fell 0.2 percent, revised up from the initially reported 0.5 percent drop, the report said.
"Growth continues at a pretty decent pace," Ryding said. "There is no doubt in my mind that there is absolutely nothing wrong with the economy."
He noted that the improvement in production indicates no inventory overhang, and that business equipment production remains strong.

"Non-auto manufacturing is quite respectable," added Sally Kleinman, economist at Chase Securities Inc. She pointed to a 0.6 percent rise in output excluding autos and auto parts in November, which followed a 0.2 percent gain in October.
Economists agreed that the production numbers do not change their view that the economy continued to grow at about a 2.5 percent pace in the fourth quarter.
That relatively healthy growth also reinforces the bond market's perception that the Fed will not be lowering interest rates anytime soon, analysts said.
"There is no way the Fed is going to be easing, but there is nothing here to say the Fed should be tightening either," Ryding said.
He noted the capacity rate, at 83.3 percent, is still a bit lower than the 83.5 percent rate seen a few months ago.

Meanwhile, the bond market reacted negatively to this morning's data. The 30-year bond fell to 98-20/32, down 12/32 from late Friday and down from 98-24/32 just prior to the production report's release.
Analysts noted that market players had been looking for an excuse to sell Treasuries in hopes of fattening yields ahead of the two-year and five-year note auctions slated for later in the week.
